Simulate a Response From a Written Model

Source: R/rstatmod.R
rstatmod.Rd

Takes a formula and a distribution, draws coefficients or uses the ones given, and returns the data drawn from that model together with the truth behind it.

Usage

rstatmod(
  formula,
  distrib,
  data = NULL,
  n = NULL,
  n_sim = 1,
  par = NULL,
  sd = 1,
  offsets = NULL,
  covariates = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

The model formula, as statmod() takes it, with the equations separated by |. Its left-hand side must be a symbol.

distrib

A distributions7 distribution object, which determines how many equations there are and the distribution from which the data are drawn.

data

A data frame of covariates, or NULL where n is given.

n

The number of observations, a positive whole number. It is required where data is NULL, and where data is given it must equal the number of rows.

n_sim

How many data sets to draw, a positive whole number. The default is 1.

par

Optional named list of what to hold, over the whole model: a distribution parameter, one of its coefficients or a group of them, a structural term's own parameter or a group of those. Each entry is a numeric vector, a single number or a function of the count. See the details. NULL, the default, draws everything.

sd

The width of the draws, 1 by default. A quantity that rides a chart (a structural parameter, a prior's own scale) is drawn at half of it, because a chart carries a width of one onto most of its parameter's range.

offsets

Optional named list of offsets, one per parameter, as statmod() takes them.

covariates

Optional named list of functions of the observation count, one per covariate, drawn afresh at every replicate. A drawn factor should have its levels fixed, since a replicate that loses a level stops the simulation with an error.

Value

An object of class "StatmodSim", a list with the elements:

data

the data frame, to which the response column has been added under the name of the formula's left-hand side.

par

the coefficients used, drawn or given, named as the design names them.

theta

the distribution's parameters at every observation, a named list with one vector per parameter.

latent

what a term with state drew (the filtered level of a score-driven term, the states of a latent chain, or the positions of a marginal break-point term), or NULL.

structural

such a term's own parameters, or NULL.

hyper

a data frame of the hyperparameters, with one row per penalty and name; each row gives the value drawn or held. Its columns are those of hyper() as far as they mean the same thing, and value takes the place of estimate, so a study compares the two directly.

n_sim

the number of data sets, as an integer.

call

the matched call.

With n_sim > 1 the fields data and theta are lists of that length, and latent is such a list when the model has a term with state and NULL otherwise; par, structural and hyper stay single.

What it is for

Simulated data have a known truth: write the model, draw from it, fit it back, and see whether the fit recovers what was put in. That is the shape of a simulation study, and of a check on a term that has just been written.

This is not stats::simulate(), which draws from a model already fitted. The r prefix is the one that R uses for a random draw, so the two names stay apart.

A covariate needs no declaration. A factor becomes its contrasts and a numeric variable stays as it is, and the design is built by the interpreter that a fit uses.

The returned truth

A simulation study compares against the coefficients, the parameters that they gave and whatever a term with state drew, so the result is a list holding all of them. Pass sim$data where a data frame is wanted.

The truth is kept as elements of a list and not as attributes of the data frame, because an attribute is not subset with the rows: sim[1:10, ] would keep a theta of the original length, while subset() and merge() drop it.

Assembly of the predictor

The predictor is built through statmod_design_at(), so the simulated data come from the model that was written and not from a linearization of it.

A term whose block moves with its coefficients, modelterms7::seg(), modelterms7::jseg() or modelterms7::nl(), contributes term_value() at the coefficients supplied, not its block times them. The two differ by the whole nonlinearity, and the simulation uses the first.

Data, or a row count

data carries the covariates. A model with none, a pure time series say, needs only n. One of the two must be given, and where both are given they must agree.

Fixed covariates or drawn ones

covariates takes one function of the observation count per column, as an entry of par may be, and the columns are drawn afresh at every replicate. A column of data under the same name is overwritten, and the columns of data that are not drawn are the same in every replicate.

The choice determines what a study measures. With data the covariates are the same throughout, so the study measures the behavior of the estimator conditional on that design; with covariates it measures that behavior over the design as well. The two choices are equally correct, and a study should state which one it ran.

A drawn factor should have its levels fixed. A factor drawn with free levels can lose a level at some replicate. The design then has another shape than the one for which the coefficients were drawn, and the simulation stops at that replicate with an error.

Several replicates

n_sim draws that many data sets. The truth is drawn once and shared by the replicates: a study over replicates measures the variability of an estimator at a given set of parameters, so the replicates differ in what is random and not in what is being estimated. Varying the truth as well requires a loop over calls and reads differently.

With n_sim > 1 the per-replicate fields data and theta come back as lists of that length, and latent does so when the model has a term with state (otherwise it is NULL), while par, structural and hyper stay single.

The quantities that are drawn

If the user names no quantity, the call draws the whole truth, so writing the model is enough to get data from it. Each quantity is drawn by the component that defines its meaning:

  • a coefficient of a design column has no other owner and comes from rnorm(1, 0, sd), which on the link scale gives predictors of order one;

  • a coordinate that some penalty covers is drawn from that penalty read as a prior, through penalties7::penalty_draw(). A Gaussian random effect gives Gaussian effects, a lasso Laplace ones and a heavy-tailed prior heavy-tailed ones. The prior's own scale is drawn as well, on the chart that the penalty carries for it, and comes back in hyper;

  • a structural term's own parameters are drawn by the term, through modelterms7::term_draw(), on the chart that each one rides. A loading stays positive and a persistence stationary whatever comes out;

  • a coefficient of a design column whose meaning only the term defines is drawn by the term, through modelterms7::term_coef_draw(), last of all, so that the values that it writes survive. A break-point is such a coordinate: it is a position on the covariate's own axis, so a normal of width sd often lands outside the data, and the term then confines it, which pins it to an edge of the interval, where one of the two segments holds a small share of the rows.

A hyperparameter that the term holds is used and not drawn, so s(x, bspline_smooth(), hyper = c(lambda = 2)) simulates at the smoothing parameter that it names. If a term draws the coordinates that a prior covers, the prior is reported at the width that the term used, since those values are no longer the prior's own draw. They are drawn Gaussian at that width, so a heavy-tailed prior over a break-point keeps its family for the fitting but not for the simulation.

A coordinate that a prior does not reach falls back to the plain draw. The cases are SCAD and MCP, which are improper by construction; an anisotropic tensor smooth, which is flat along its null space; a covariance class spanning a filter and an equation at once, which is in neither vector on its own; and a coordinate for which the draw of the penalty is missing.

Fixing quantities by name

par is one named list over the whole model, and a key may be

  • a distribution parameter, mu, which is that whole equation;

  • one of its coefficients or a group of them, mu.(Intercept) or mu.random, where a group is a name that the members extend at a dot;

  • a structural term's own parameter, kappa1, or a group of those, omega.random.

A value is a vector of that key's own length, a single number used for all of them, or a function of the count. A function writes a structured truth without a vocabulary of its own: function(k) rnorm(k, 0, 0.4) is a random effect at a scale chosen by the caller and function(k) c(1.5, -2, rep(0, k - 2)) is a sparse truth for a lasso to find. A function that returns the wrong number of values or a missing value is rejected, because R would recycle a vector of the wrong length into a different model. A key that addresses nothing is rejected with a message that lists what the model does carry.

A structural parameter is named on the scale of modelterms7::term_params(): a loading is the loading and not its logarithm, and a persistence is the partial autocorrelation that its chart carries. A parameter that a subformula develops is different. Its coordinates are the coefficients of that development, which act on the unconstrained scale of the parameter's own chart, so kappa1 is a loading and kappa1.random.3 is a group's departure on the log scale that the loading rides. This keeps every group's loading positive whatever the departure is.

A term with state

The simulation runs through modelterms7::term_simulate(), so the recursion that generates the data is the term's own. A score-driven term draws the response as it runs, and its level at one time is driven by the score at the time before; a latent chain draws its path from the stationary law with which the likelihood is written; a marginal break-point term draws each group's positions from their prior. The values that each term drew come back in latent, and a recovery check compares a fit with them.

The parameters of such a term are not coefficients of any equation. They are named in par beside the equations' coefficients, and since a formula holds at most one such term, the names carry no term key. They are drawn like every other coefficient.

The response's name

The left-hand side of the formula must be a symbol. log(y) ~ x is rejected because the model generates values of log(y), which cannot be stored in a column under either name. A censored response is rejected too, for the reason that statmod() rejects one: there is no censored likelihood.

See also

statmod() to fit what this draws, simulate.StatmodFit() to draw from a model already fitted, print.StatmodSim() for the printed form.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(50), g = factor(rep(c("a", "b"), 25)))

# The coefficients are drawn.
sim <- rstatmod(y ~ x + g, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
sim$par
#> $mu
#>  (Intercept)            x           gb 
#>  0.291446236 -0.443291873  0.001105352 
#> 
#> $sigma
#> (Intercept) 
#>  0.07434132 
#> 

# The coefficients are given, and a fit recovers them.
sim2 <- rstatmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd,
                 par = list(mu = c(1, 2), sigma = log(0.3)))
coef(statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), sim2$data))
#> $mu
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>    1.030843    1.935854 
#> 
#> $sigma
#> (Intercept) 
#>   -1.145181 
#> 

# A sparse truth is written as a function of the coefficient count.
dd2 <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(50 * 6), 50, 6))
sim3 <- rstatmod(y ~ lasso(~ V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5 + V6),
                 distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd2,
                 par = list(mu = function(k) c(2, -1.5, rep(0, k - 2)),
                            sigma = log(0.3)))
head(sim3$data$y, 3)
#> [1] 2.108603 3.625229 6.596983

# This model has no covariates at all.
sim4 <- rstatmod(y ~ 1, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), n = 20)
nrow(sim4$data)
#> [1] 20

# A study over replicates draws the covariates afresh at each one.
study <- rstatmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), n = 80,
                  n_sim = 5, par = list(mu = c(1, 2), sigma = log(0.5)),
                  covariates = list(x = function(n) runif(n, -2, 2)))
length(study$data)
#> [1] 5
vapply(study$data, function(d) coef(statmod(
  y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), d),
  readable = FALSE)$mu[[2L]], numeric(1))
#> [1] 2.017968 2.036897 2.013920 2.043438 1.935684

# In a score-driven series, the term's own parameters are named beside the
# equations'.
sim5 <- rstatmod(y ~ 0 + gas(p = 1, q = 1, time = t),
                 distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(),
                 data.frame(t = 1:100),
                 par = list(sigma = 0, omega = 0.4, kappa1 = 0.3,
                            pacf1 = 0.6))
head(sim5$latent, 3)
#> [1] 1.0000000 0.6960904 0.6137012

# In a panel whose level varies by group, naming nothing draws the
# deviations from the prior that random() declares, at a scale drawn too.
pan <- data.frame(id = factor(rep(1:6, each = 10)), t = rep(1:10, 6))
sim6 <- rstatmod(y ~ 0 + gas(p = 1, q = 1, omega ~ 1 + random(~1 | id),
                             by = id, time = t),
                 distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), pan)
sim6$hyper
#>   parameter                                                              term
#> 1        mu gas(p = 1, q = 1, omega ~ 1 + random(~1 | id), by = id, time = t)
#>    name     value  held
#> 1 sigma 0.6269308 FALSE
length(unique(round(sim6$theta$mu, 6))) > 6
#> [1] TRUE
